```{r hexlogo, echo=FALSE, fig.align="right", out.width="110px", fig.alt="annotatR logo"}
knitr::include_graphics("../man/figures/logo.png")
```

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(annotatR)
```

Annotations are only useful if they can leave the tool that made them. annotatR
stores every region of interest as a validated simple-feature geometry in image
pixel coordinates, with an explicit pyramid level attached, which makes it
straightforward to hand work off to a viewer such as QuPath, to a GIS-flavoured
GeoJSON consumer, or to a Python segmentation pipeline, and to take the results
back again. Because the geometry model is the same one used internally, an
export followed by an import is a genuine round-trip rather than a lossy
approximation, and this vignette shows a live one for each format so you can see
that labels, identities, and coordinates survive intact.

A guiding principle runs through all four formats below: the coordinate
convention never changes silently. Coordinates are written in image pixels
unless you deliberately ask otherwise, so a polygon you exported lands back on
exactly the same pixels when you read it in.

We use the bundled example project throughout: three labelled rectangles on a
small tissue raster.

```{r project}
proj <- at_example_project()
at_rois(proj)[, c("roi_id", "layer", "label", "geom_type", "area_px")]
```

## GeoJSON

`at_write_geojson()` serialises a project to a standard `FeatureCollection`.
Each ROI becomes one `Feature` whose `geometry` is the pixel-coordinate polygon
and whose `properties` carry the full annotatR schema: `roi_id`, `layer`,
`label`, `level`, `source_level`, `author`, `created`, `modified`, `source`, the writing
`annotatR_version`, and any free-form `attributes`. Keeping the schema explicit
is what lets a file survive a return trip.

```{r geojson-write}
gj <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
at_write_geojson(proj, gj)
cat(readLines(gj)[1:22], sep = "\n")
```

The `roi_id` is preserved verbatim, so an ROI keeps its identity across the
boundary and you can join exported measurements back to the original
annotation. Reading the file back with `at_read_geojson()` reconstructs one
`annot_layer` per distinct `layer` property. We rebuild a project on the
original image and check that the labels came through intact.

```{r geojson-roundtrip}
back <- at_read_geojson(gj)
imported <- at_project(proj$image, back[["regions"]])
identical(sort(at_rois(proj)$label), sort(at_rois(imported)$label))
```

### Coordinate levels and legacy imports

GeoJSON and QuPath exports write `level` matching their coordinates, with the
stored ROI level in `source_level` as provenance. The
`coordinate_schema = "annotatR-pixel-level-v1"` marker identifies this corrected
contract. CSV exports always use level-0 coordinates and `level = 0`. Image
dimensions determine separate x/y scale factors; no power-of-two pyramid is
inferred. Vector geometry round trips use floating-point precision (relative
tolerance `1e-12`); supported raster-mask round trips preserve integer pixels
on the same pixel grid.

Some older exports paired level-0 geometry with a nonzero stored ROI level.
Those files cannot be distinguished reliably from valid nonzero-coordinate
files. Readers reject unmarked nonzero recorded levels by default with an
interpretation error. To explicitly trust legitimate recorded-level foreign or
legacy files, pass `legacy_levels = "recorded"`. When the actual coordinate
level is independently known, use `coordinate_level = 0L` (or the known level)
with `at_read_geojson()`, `at_read_rois_csv()`, or `at_read_qupath()`. This explicit
import mode overrides the level declaration without scaling coordinates. Use
either mode only when the coordinate convention is known; do not guess a repair. Missing level metadata defaults to level 0, or
the reader's explicit fallback `level` where supported.

Mask imports (including NPY) recover the level from the RDS object or legend
sidecar by default; an explicit `level` overrides it. Preserve the sidecar alongside raster files.
For unannotated external masks, supply the known level when it is not 0.

### The `flip_y` option

annotatR's convention is image orientation: the origin is top-left and *y*
increases downward. Many GIS tools instead expect *y* to increase upward. Set
`flip_y = TRUE` to write coordinates in that upward convention; the y-axis is
mirrored about the image height. If you write flipped, you must read flipped,
supplying the same `height` so the inversion is undone:

```{r geojson-flip}
h <- at_dims(proj$image)[2]
gj_flip <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
at_write_geojson(proj, gj_flip, flip_y = TRUE)
regained <- at_read_geojson(gj_flip, flip_y = TRUE, height = h)
identical(sort(at_rois(at_project(proj$image, regained[["regions"]]))$centroid_y),
          sort(at_rois(proj)$centroid_y))
```

Leave `flip_y` at its default `FALSE` when exchanging with other
image-coordinate tools (including QuPath and annotatR itself); reach for it only
when a downstream consumer explicitly wants a cartesian, bottom-left origin.

## QuPath

QuPath reads and writes its own GeoJSON dialect. `at_write_qupath()` emits
current `objectType` and `classification.color` RGB arrays, preserving labels,
colours and lock state. `at_read_qupath()` accepts native Feature arrays,
FeatureCollections and single Features, with both current fields and legacy
`object_type`/`colorRGB` fields. Null classifications become `"unclassified"`.
Malformed fields and conflicting declarations are rejected explicitly.

```{r qupath-write}
qp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
at_write_qupath(proj, qp)
```

QuPath requires UUID feature IDs. annotatR keeps existing UUIDs and derives a
deterministic UUID for other IDs, while recording the original ID in
`properties.metadata.annotatR_roi_id`. The same string metadata map retains
`annotatR_coordinate_schema` and `annotatR_coordinate_level`. Native QuPath
0.7.0 retains these entries through import/export; annotatR recovers the original
ID on return. If another tool removes this metadata, a non-UUID original ID
cannot be recovered from the native UUID. Ordinary external feature IDs are
preserved. Identical repeated metadata emitted by QuPath 0.7.0 is accepted;
contradictory repeated mappings and duplicate recovered IDs fail explicitly.

Annotation and detection kinds are supported. Imported objects use the ROI
source `"imported"`, and retain their kind in `attributes$qupath_object_type`
so detections remain detections on re-export. Other QuPath kinds, including
cells with separate nucleus geometry, are rejected rather than simplified.
Mask/derived ROIs without an imported kind export as detections; other ROIs
export as annotations. Image coordinate geometry is preserved, including holes.

```{r qupath-read}
lyr <- at_read_qupath(qp)
lyr$style$colour
```

## Masks for Python

For pixel-level pipelines the exchange currency is a raster mask, not a polygon.
`at_write_mask()` writes an integer TIFF alongside a self-describing
`<path>.legend.json` sidecar that records the mask type, level, dimensions, and
one entry per class (`value`, `label`, `layer`, `roi_id`, `n_px`, `colour`). The
sidecar is what turns an anonymous grid of integers into something a downstream
model can interpret without guessing which value meant which class, and it
travels with the raster so the mapping is never lost.

```{r mask-write}
m <- at_mask(proj, type = "labelled")
mp <- tempfile(fileext = ".tiff")
at_write_mask(m, mp)
cat(readLines(paste0(mp, ".legend.json"))[1:14], sep = "\n")
```

Here we used a `"labelled"` mask, where each ROI gets its own integer; a
`"binary"` mask collapses everything to foreground and background, and a
`"multiclass"` mask shares one integer per label. Whichever you choose, the
legend describes exactly what the pixels mean. On the Python side, read the TIFF
as an integer array and load the legend to map values back to labels. This chunk
is illustrative and is not run when the vignette is built.

```python
import json
import numpy as np
import tifffile

mask = tifffile.imread("mask.tiff")
with open("mask.tiff.legend.json") as f:
    legend = json.load(f)

labels = {e["value"]: e["label"] for e in legend["legend"]}
for value, label in labels.items():
    print(label, int(np.sum(mask == value)), "px")
```

## CSV and WKT

For spreadsheet users and pipelines that would rather not parse JSON,
`at_write_rois_csv()` produces one row per ROI with the geometry in a
Well-Known Text `geometry` column, plus the metadata fields. `at_read_rois_csv()`
parses any CSV with at least `label` and `geometry` columns back into a layer.

```{r csv}
csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
at_write_rois_csv(proj, csv)
lyr_csv <- at_read_rois_csv(csv, layer_name = "regions")
at_rois(at_project(proj$image, lyr_csv))[, c("label", "geom_type", "area_px")]
```

Because WKT is understood by PostGIS, `sf`, Shapely, and most spatial
databases, the CSV is often the shortest path into a wider geospatial stack.

For the complete list of import and export helpers, see the reference index on
the package website.


## Use of LLM tools

Portions of this package were prepared with assistance from large language model tooling for narrowly defined, non-authorial tasks: copyediting, prose smoothing, Markdown/LaTeX formatting, scaffolding of boilerplate files (CI configs, build scripts), code refactoring. The tools used were Chat AI, the LLM service of KISSKI (GWDG), and a self-hosted Mistral Small (24B, Apache-2.0) run locally via Ollama and the ollamar R package — local inference only, with no data sent to third parties for the self-hosted model.


## Export destinations and receipts

Batch and split-mask exports turn project, layer, ROI and class names into safe
portable filename components and append deterministic suffixes for collisions.
Display labels remain in receipts and annotation/legend metadata. Package and
app exports preflight the complete bundle, including sidecars and receipt files,
and reject symlinked descendants before writing. An explicitly selected
single-file output path can point to any caller-chosen directory.

A mask and its legend are staged before either is published. Existing bundles
are skipped unless replacement was requested, and a failed item does not prevent
later items from running. Receipts include every requested item with `ok`,
`error` or `skipped`, a message, paths and double-precision byte counts for both
output and sidecar. `ok` means the whole requested bundle was published. A
failed publication restores prior files; if restoration fails, the error names
the retained backup. Session exports replace `_export_manifest.csv` and
`_annotation_summary.csv` each run. Receipt/summary failures warn, remain in
receipt attributes, and do not discard the returned item outcomes. App downloads
include the receipt and all complete bundles, and display failure/skip counts.

Writers must be serialized and destination paths kept stable during an export.
Preflight and several filesystem renames do not provide a race-free transaction
against concurrent writers, crashes between renames, or hostile symlink changes.
